newsitem.title: USA: Dlr starts sharply lower in U.S., below 114 yen. [CORRECTED 14:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Dlr starts sharply lower in U.S., below 114 yen. [CORRECTED 14:30 GMT]

text.p: The dollar opened sharply weaker versus the yen but above overseas lows amid lingering concern about prospects for increases in Japan's official discount rate (ODR) and trade surplus, currency experts said.

"As long as that fear is out there, that's going to keep being traded off even though it may never come to fruition any time soon," said David Ethridge, director of currency analysis in North America at MMS International. "Fears move markets." Ethridge was referring to concern about a Japan rate hike. The Bank of Japan (BOJ) has kept its ODR at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995.

The greenback had tumbled in Europe to 111.98 yen, its lowest level since December 1996 after reports on Tuesday that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) was considering making a recommendation to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Japan raise its ODR.
Later that day, Jiji news agency reported that a key LDP official said now is not the time for the BOJ to tighten credit.
Jiji also quoted Taku Yamasaki, chairman of the LDP policy research council as saying it was inappropriate to discuss the possibility of a rise in the ODR now.

The yen's huge gain (corrects from drop) spurred remarks from Eisuke Sakakibara, the director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau. He told Reuters on Tuesday that the pace of the yen's strengthening is too rapid.

The dollar had bounced off the bottom in Europe. By the start of U.S. trade, the beleaguered greenback fetched 113.60/70 yen, still well below Monday's closing level of 115.57/67. Against the German mark, the dollar slid to 1.6970/80 from 1.7075/85.
Japan's trade surplus more than doubled in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday the rise in the surplus was temporary and unlikely to become a major issue with other countries.
Still Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York, emphasized the important point is that Mitsuzuka admitted Japan's surplus was increasing.
"So, that's why the market reacted by selling the dollar against yen," Igarashi said. He noted there were huge selling orders overseas.

In other trading, the dollar opened at 1.4065/75 Swiss francs, down from 1.4270/80 francs at the previous close. Sterling rose to $1.6437/47 from $1.6390/00. The dollar inched up to Canadian $1.3725/30 from C$1.3713/18. The Australian dollar opened at $0.7723/28, down from $0.7742/47.
Beyond concerns about Japanese rates and economic fundamentals, the market focused on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting that began Tuesday at 1300 GMT.

The latest Reuters poll released Monday showed 21 U.S. primary dealers expected rates to be left unchanged, while 18 predicted a 25 basis point rise in the 5.50 percent federal funds rate. Of that 18, three forecasted the Fed would also lift the 5.0 percent discount rate.

Should the FOMC tighten, Ruesch International market analyst Brian McCarthy said, "There is so much uncertainty in the market, I think, the reaction would be fairly straight forward in that the short-term reaction would be dollar negative, with the stock and bond prices coming off."
But eventually, the focus would shift to the interest rate spreads and that would give the dollar a boost by the end of the day, particularly for dollar/yen, McCarthy said.
